import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Convexity-aware risk: how much placing the job on a machine raises the *variance-tilted* max of machine loads, i.e. the expected makespan under a softmax over loads whose temperature equals the empirical job-size spread."""
    m = len(loads)
    if past_jobs.size >= 2:
        mu = float(np.mean(past_jobs))
        sd = float(np.std(past_jobs))
    else:
        mu = float(job)
        sd = float(job) if job > 0 else 1.0
    # temperature of the softmax: proportional to remaining-work uncertainty per machine
    temp = sd * np.sqrt(max(jobs_left, 1) / m) + 1e-9
    new_loads = loads + job
    # soft-max (log-sum-exp) of loads behaves like expected max; its sensitivity to a
    # candidate is the softmax probability, but we use the CURVATURE-weighted shift:
    z_old = (loads - np.max(loads)) / temp
    z_new = (new_loads - np.max(new_loads)) / temp
    p_old = np.exp(z_old); p_old /= p_old.sum()
    p_new = np.exp(z_new); p_new /= p_new.sum()
    # change in the softmax-distribution mass above the mean load
    above_old = p_old[None, :]  # placeholder shape keeps vectorised
    # per-candidate: how much this machine's own softmax mass shifts, weighted by load
    shift = (p_new - p_old)  # length m, sums to 0
    # score: negative shift in tail mass beyond the mean (avoid loading the currently-likely-max machine)
    tail = (loads > np.mean(loads)).astype(float)
    score = -(shift @ tail)
    scale = np.max(np.abs(score)) + 1e-9
    return score / scale

feature.name: huge_occupancy_guard

idea.hypothesis: Everything per machine is inferred from one number (its load), so 'is this machine already carrying a huge job?' can only be a threshold on load. A sparse step (1/(1+exp(-(load-tau)/w)) with tau = 0.4*max(past)), switched on only when the arriving job is huge on a LOG size scale, forbids a second huge job on an occupied machine. If the bimodal excess (280 vs LB 199) is huge-job stacking, this alone must lower the bottleneck; if it is flat, stacking is not the failure and the extra load is small-job mass.

feature.name: mode_split_pad_hinge
feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Job-size-split pad hinge: huge arrivals take the emptiest machine, small arrivals are repelled only from machines below the mean post-load."""
    m = len(loads)
    post = loads + job
    scale = max(loads) + job + 1.0
    huge = -(post - np.min(post)) / scale
    small = -np.maximum(np.mean(post) - post, 0.0) / scale
    if past_jobs.size < 8:
        g = 0.0
    else:
        g = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(np.log(job + 1.0) - np.log(np.mean(past_jobs) + 1.0))))
    return g * huge + (1.0 - g) * small

idea.hypothesis: The bimodal bottleneck (280 = 199 + ~81) looks like landing pads being eaten: least-load sends tiny jobs onto the only free machines, so a late huge job lands on filler. One feature with a job-size sign split: huge arrivals score -post (take the emptiest machine), small arrivals score -relu(mean(post)-post), i.e. they are repelled only from machines BELOW the mean and are indifferent above it. Pads therefore stay empty while huge jobs are still possible, without feeding the current top. Signature of the mechanism: loads polarise (pads near 0, carriers high).
idea.feature: m=len(loads). past_jobs.size<8 -> g=0 else g = the same log gate as huge_occupancy_guard. scale=max(loads)+job+1; post=loads+job; huge=-(post-min(post))/scale; small=-maximum(mean(post)-post,0)/scale; return g*huge+(1-g)*small (one column, roughly [-1,1]).
idea.lesson: f011 had the sign flip but its small-job side was still 'go to the emptiest', i.e. f002 again; the small side must be indifferent to the top, not attracted to it.

feature.coder_note: This computes a single column: a logistic gate `g` on the arriving job's log size relative to the mean past log size (0 when fewer than 8 past jobs), blending `huge = -(post - min(post))/scale` (favour the emptiest machine) for large arrivals with `small = -relu(mean(post) - post)/scale` (repel onl…

feature.name: size_gated_pad_reserve
feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Heavy-tail-gated mix: huge jobs prefer the emptiest machine, small jobs penalise the k lightest machines (pads)."""
    m = len(loads)
    if past_jobs.size < 8:
        return np.zeros(m)
    mx = float(np.max(past_jobs))
    med = float(np.median(past_jobs))
    ht = float(np.clip((np.log1p(mx) - np.log1p(max(med, 1e-9))) / 2.0, 0.0, 1.0))
    g = ht
    post = loads + job
    scale = float(np.max(post)) + 1.0
    huge = -(post - np.min(post)) / scale
    k = max(1, m // 10)
    Lk = float(np.partition(loads, k - 1)[k - 1])
    w = 0.05 * (abs(Lk) + job + 1.0)
    pad = np.clip((Lk + w - loads) / w, 0.0, 1.0)
    small = -pad
    return ht * (g * huge + (1.0 - g) * small)

idea.hypothesis: Push the huge side toward EXCLUSIVE empty machines by building the pads explicitly: for small arrivals, penalise the k=max(1,m//10) lightest machines (hard top-k, not a soft count), so they stay at ~0 and any later huge job is the only occupant. Large arrivals still take the emptiest. Multiplied by a heavy-tail gate (log max/median of past sizes) so it fires in bimodal/exponential and is harmless in uniform. If pads are the mechanism, the bimodal makespan falls from 280 toward 199+small.
idea.feature: m=len(loads). If past_jobs.size<8 return zeros(m). mx=max(past_jobs), med=median(past_jobs); ht=clip((log1p(mx)-log1p(max(med,1e-9)))/2.0,0,1); g = same log gate as before. post=loads+job; scale=max(post)+1; huge=-(post-min(post))/scale. k=max(1,m//10); Lk=float(np.partition(loads,k-1)[k-1]); w=0.05*(abs(Lk)+job+1.0); pad=clip((Lk+w-loads)/w,0,1) (1 on the k lightest); small=-pad; return ht*(g*huge+(1-g)*small).
idea.lesson: f020 (reserve the sole empty machine) was flat because 'load==0' almost never holds; a hard top-k on the k lightest always bites.

feature.measures: Heavy-tail-gated mix: huge jobs prefer the emptiest machine, small jobs penalise the k lightest machines (pads).

prediction.why: not checked: the feature made the policy much worse at every weight tried

feature.name: huge_tail_softmax_charge

idea.hypothesis: Charge each machine the future huge load it will actually absorb: total remaining huge work (huge_rate*jobs_left*huge_avg from the past) times a softmax over emptiness, so the emptiest machines carry the biggest charge. The charge is calibrated to the current load spread (C = 0.8*spread/(max(p)-min(p))), which puts the peak of post+C*p in the mid-band instead of at either extreme, and the whole term decays to zero as jobs_left -> 0, so the tail shapes the projection and the endgame reverts to least-loaded.
idea.feature: m=len(loads). If past_jobs.size<10 or jobs_left<=0 return zeros(m). mx=max(past_jobs), med=median(past_jobs), thr=max(0.5*mx,3.0*med), mask=past_jobs>=thr; if not any(mask) return zeros(m). huge_left=mean(mask)*jobs_left; huge_avg=mean(past_jobs[mask]); total=huge_left*huge_avg; if total<=0 return zeros(m). post=loads+job; T=max(mean(loads)+job,1.0); z=clip(-loads/T,-60,0); p=exp(z); p=p/sum(p). spread=max(loads)-min(loads)+job; C=min(0.8*spread/(max(p)-min(p)+1e-9), total); s=-(post+C*p); return s/(max(abs(s))+1e-9).
idea.lesson: f042's reservation depth was tanh-squashed and monotone in slack, so it re-ranked like f002 and lost on validation; here the charge is calibrated to the load spread so the ranking peaks strictly inside the load range.

nodes.title: relative load
nodes.description: Score by minus load divided by the arriving job size, favouring machines where this job is proportionally cheap.

argued.argument: Not inert (varies with loads), not a duplicate of f002 (rho 0.979, not exact), and not a span of kept features: the abs() around loads+job-mx is nonlinear and cannot be reproduced by any linear combination of f002, f005, f039.

nodes.description: Estimate the final average load from total work plus remaining jobs and score machines by how far below that target they are.

nodes.title: size-aware placement
nodes.description: Route large jobs toward empty machines and small jobs toward least-loaded, using job size relative to the mean past size.

nodes.title: nonlinear load pressure
nodes.description: Score by a convex transform of load (e.g. negative load squared or exponential) to penalise already-heavy machines more sharply.

notes.result: not attempted: no feature under it is close to a duplicate or to the kept features (nearest rho < 0.93, R^2 < 0.98)

nodes.title: size-gated routing
nodes.description: Use a nonlinear gate on job size relative to observed sizes to switch between pure least-loaded (small jobs) and empty-machine-first (large jobs), so the two regimes are not a linear blend.

nodes.title: big-job reservation
nodes.description: Track the largest job seen and keep at least one machine near-empty as a landing pad for future large jobs, penalising filling the last empty machine with small work.

nodes.title: tail-aware projected finish
nodes.description: Projected finish where the future-work estimate per machine uses the empirical upper tail (max/quantile of past sizes times jobs_left) rather than the mean, so big arrivals are anticipated.

nodes.title: bimodal reservation depth
nodes.description: Score machines by how many large jobs their remaining capacity could still absorb, given the observed frequency of large jobs.

nodes.title: capacity-slot reservation
nodes.description: Score machines by how many future large jobs their remaining capacity could absorb, given the observed frequency and size of large jobs.

nodes.title: bimodal two-mode split
nodes.description: Explicitly classify the arriving job as tiny or huge relative to the empirical size distribution and use a different ranking rule in each mode.

nodes.title: huge-job count balance
nodes.description: For upper-tail arriving jobs, penalise machines already carrying an inferred huge job, so the ~18 huge jobs land on distinct machines instead of stacking.

nodes.title: bound-excess penalty
nodes.description: Score only the part of a machine's post-placement load above the estimated reachable bound max(average, largest job, tail pair), so machines below the bound tie and attention goes to real bottlenecks.
